items.title: CVE-2025-62859 - Block processing stall via witness malleation
items.desc: Block processing in Bitcoin Core before versions 29.2 and 30.0 may be stalled by a malicious peer exploiting witness malleation in compact blocks, under some conditions. This issue is considered Medium severity. Details Affected Bitcoin Core versions would clear download state for a compact block following reconstruction, but prior to checking for witness malleation. If that check failed, the node would fallback to requesting the block to the same peer via GETDATA, with a 10 minutes timeout. A malicious peer, when it announces a compact block to a victim first, could leverage this defect to stall the victim’s block processing. If the attacker controlled the victim’s 3 high-bandwidth peers, or if the victim was running with -blocksonly, this could be repeated indefinitely. Attribution Eugene Siegel discovered this issue and responsibly disclosed it. Timeline 2025-04-28 Eugene reports this issue to the Bitcoin Core security list 2025-05-30 Gregory Sanders open PR #32646 to fix this issue 2025-06-30 PR #32646 is merged 2025-09-12 PR #32646 is backported to version 29 2025-10-10 Bitcoin Core 30.0 is released with a fix 2025-10-14 Bitcoin Core 29.2 is released with a fix 2026-10-27 The last vulnerable Bitcoin Core version (29.x) goes end of life 2026-11-10 Public disclosure.

items.title: CVE-2025-62860 - Inbound Tor connections wrongly receive -whitelist permissions
items.desc: Bitcoin Core before versions 28.3, 29.2 and 30.0 will also include Tor inbound peers in a whitelist configured over an IP range. This issue is considered Medium severity. Details In Bitcoin Core, the IP address of inbound Tor peers is that of the Tor daemon, which usually runs on the same machine or local network. The -whitelist configuration lifts various DoS limits and privacy leak mitigations for trusted peers. Bitcoin Core would whitelist inbound Tor connections if the address of the Tor proxy would match the IP range configured via the -whitelist option. Inbound Tor connections received on an onion bind are never whitelisted in Bitcoin Core 30.0 and all later versions, as well as 28.3 and later minor versions and 29.2 and later minor versions. Nodes that did not set the non-default -whitelist option were never affected. Popular vendors bundled Bitcoin Core with a Tor daemon, and set the -whitelist option to an IP range matching that of the Tor daemon. The -whitelist option was also an operational requirement for client software of Bitcoin Core, which was commonly run alongside a Tor daemon. This led to thousands of reachable mainnet nodes whitelisting all incoming Tor connections. Attribution Martin Zumsande and Antoine Poinsot discovered the issue and responsibly disclosed it. Timeline 2025-09-12 Martin and Antoine report this issue to the Bitcoin Core security team 2025-09-15 Martin opens PR #33395 to stop considering Tor inbound peers when applying whitelist permissions 2025-09-17 Antoine reports this issue to Bitcoin Knots maintainer Luke Dashjr, who acknowledges it on the same day 2025-09-17 PR #33395 is merged and backported to previous releases 2025-09-19 Antoine reports this issue to several software providers affected 2025-10-10 Bitcoin Core 30.0 is released with a fix 2025-10-14 Bitcoin Core 29.2 is released with a fix 2025-10-20 Bitcoin Core 28.3 is released with a fix 2026-10-27 The last vulnerable Bitcoin Core version (29.x) goes end of life 2026-11-10 Public disclosure.

items.title: CVE-2025-62861 - Block template creation halted by TRUC sibling eviction during reorg
items.desc: Disclosure of the details of a mempool inconsistency due to TRUC “sibling eviction” rules firing on reorg. A fix was released on October 10th 2025 in Bitcoin Core v30.0. Affected versions are 28.0 to 28.2 and 29.0 to 29.1. This issue is considered High severity. Details Transaction relay policy applies extra topology restrictions to version 3 (“TRUC”) transactions (see BIP 431): a TRUC transaction may have at most one unconfirmed ancestor and at most one unconfirmed descendant. These are mempool policy rules, not consensus rules, so a valid block may contain any topology, including a TRUC parent with several children. When a transaction submitted to the mempool would give a TRUC parent a second unconfirmed child, Bitcoin Core’s “sibling eviction” logic (introduced in v28.0) treats the existing child as a replacement candidate and, if the new transaction pays enough, evicts it under replace-by-fee rules. During a chain reorganization, the transactions from the disconnected blocks are re-added to the mempool with bypass_limits=true. This is meant to restore previously-confirmed transactions faithfully, without applying mempool anti-DoS or topology policy. The bug was that the sibling-eviction branch was not gated on bypass_limits, so TRUC enforcement still ran while transactions were being re-added. A reorg can restore a transaction topology that violates TRUC’s descendant limit: valid in a block but impossible to form in the mempool. Re-adding such transactions with sibling eviction still active could evict a restored transaction while leaving its in-mempool descendants behind, so the mempool held transactions spending outputs that no longer existed. The main effect of this inconsistent state is that a miner’s block template creation can no longer succeed: the assembled template fails its validity check, so a node that performed such a reorg cannot produce blocks until it is restarted, which reloads the mempool in a consistent state. This was fixed in PR #33504 by gating the TRUC checks on bypass_limits, so that sibling eviction no longer runs during reorg re-addition. Attribution Credit goes to Niklas Goegge for discovering and responsibly disclosing this issue. Timeline 2025-09-26 - Niklas Goegge reports this issue to the Bitcoin Core security mailing list 2025-09-29 - Greg Sanders opens PR #33504 with the fix 2025-10-02 - PR #33504 is merged into master 2025-10-03 - The fix is backported to the 29.x branch in PR #33474 2025-10-06 - The fix is backported to the 30.x branch in PR #33473 2025-10-07 - The fix is backported to the 28.x branch in PR #33535 2025-10-10 - Bitcoin Core 30.0 is released with a fix 2025-10-14 - Bitcoin Core 29.2 is released with a fix 2025-10-17 - Bitcoin Core 28.3 is released with a fix 2026-10-27 - The last vulnerable Bitcoin Core version (29.x) goes end of life 2026-11-10 - Public Disclosure
